name: Cherokee Kanuchi
imageAlt: Black walnuts, the defining ingredient in Cherokee kanuchi
imageCredit: Illustrative black-walnut image via Wikimedia Commons; see source page for author and license.
summary: Cherokee kanuchi, a rich black-walnut soup made by pounding shelled nuts into a paste and simmering it gently with water.
lead: Black walnuts become a creamy, deeply nutty soup through pounding and patient simmering rather than dairy or flour.
about: Kanuchi is a Cherokee black-walnut preparation traditionally made by pounding shelled nuts into a dense paste, historically with a large mortar and pestle, then simmering portions of the paste in water. Modern home cooks can reproduce the core method with a food processor while keeping the ingredient list restrained.
story: Cherokee cultural and foodway sources describe kanuchi as an enduring winter food built around native black walnuts. The labor of shelling and pounding is part of the dish's history, and community recipes vary in sweetness, thickness and whether the nut solids are strained. This version follows the publicly documented home-kitchen approach without presenting one household formula as universal.
caveat: Black walnuts are strongly flavored and different from English walnuts. This is a home adaptation of a documented Cherokee preparation; community methods vary.
prepNotes: English walnuts make a milder, different soup.
The nuts should clump and release oil, not remain coarse crumbs.
Hard boiling can make the nut solids separate harshly.
ingredients: 6 cups water, plus more as needed
1 to 2 tbsp maple syrup or sugar, optional
steps: Pulse black walnuts in a food processor until very finely ground and beginning to form an oily paste.
Checkpoint: a squeezed spoonful should hold together rather than fall apart as dry crumbs.
Bring 6 cups water to a gentle simmer in a heavy saucepan and whisk in the walnut paste a little at a time.
Simmer 35–45 minutes over low heat, stirring often and scraping the bottom.
Checkpoint: the broth should turn opaque tan-brown, smell intensely nutty and lightly coat a spoon.
Season with salt and, only if desired, a little maple syrup or sugar.
Rest 10 minutes before serving so the natural walnut oils settle back into the soup.
sources: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods
Fringe Table — Indigenous Americas foodways guide

name: Ethiopian Chechebsa
imageAlt: Illustrative Ethiopian flatbread used for chechebsa
imageCredit: Illustrative Ethiopian flatbread image via Wikimedia Commons; see source page for author/license.
summary: Chechebsa: torn Ethiopian flatbread coated with spiced butter and berbere for a warm, quick breakfast.
lead: Fresh skillet bread is torn while hot, then tossed with niter kibbeh and berbere until every piece is glossy and brick-red.
about: Chechebsa, also called kita firfir, is an Ethiopian breakfast made from a simple unleavened skillet bread torn into pieces and coated with spiced clarified butter and berbere. The pleasure comes from contrast: some pieces stay soft, others pick up toasted edges, and the spice-fat mixture reaches every surface.
story: Chechebsa belongs to a broad Ethiopian family of dishes that transform bread with seasoned fat or sauce. Unlike injera-based firfir, this version starts with fresh wheat flatbread. Breakfast versions may be served with yogurt, honey or tea depending on household and region.
caveat: Names, bread formulas and heat levels vary. This recipe uses a practical wheat-flour kita and niter kibbeh.
prepNotes: Chechebsa is best while the kita is still warm and flexible.
Blends vary dramatically; start moderate and add more at the table.
The bread should be coated, not swimming in butter.
ingredients: 2 tbsp neutral oil for the pan
Plain yogurt or honey, optional for serving
steps: Mix flour and salt, then add warm water gradually until a soft, nonsticky dough forms. Rest 10 minutes.
Roll into a round about 1/4 inch thick and cook in a lightly oiled skillet over medium heat until browned in spots on both sides and cooked through.
Checkpoint: the bread should bend without raw dough at the center and show toasted freckles.
Tear hot bread into bite-size pieces.
Melt niter kibbeh in the skillet, stir in berbere for 20–30 seconds, then add bread pieces.
Toss over low heat 2–3 minutes until evenly coated and a few edges crisp.
Serve hot, with yogurt or honey alongside if desired.
sources: Saveur — Ethiopian food and berbere cooking

name: Ghanaian Red Red
imageCredit: Image via Wikimedia Commons; see linked file page for creator and license.
summary: Ghanaian red red: black-eyed peas in a tomato, chile and red-palm-oil stew, traditionally paired with fried ripe plantain.
lead: Creamy black-eyed peas, red palm oil and tomato make a deeply colored Ghanaian stew built for sweet fried plantain.
about: Red red is a Ghanaian bean stew most often made with black-eyed peas or cowpeas, tomato, onion, chile and red palm oil. Its name is commonly linked to the reddish stew and the ripe fried plantain served beside it. The beans should be creamy but still recognizable, with oil visibly seasoning rather than flooding the sauce.
story: Red red is everyday food in Ghana and a strong example of the importance of cowpeas and palm oil in West African cooking. Street-food and home versions vary in smoked fish, chile and bean texture. This plant-forward version keeps the defining bean-tomato-palm-oil structure and serves plantain alongside.
caveat: Some Ghanaian versions include smoked fish or additional seasonings. This meatless version preserves the core bean and palm-oil character.
prepNotes: It contributes both flavor and the characteristic orange-red color.
Undercooked cowpeas make the stew feel chalky.
Yellow skins with dark spots give the sweet contrast expected beside the stew.
ingredients: 1 Scotch bonnet, left whole or minced to taste
steps: Heat palm oil over medium and cook half the onion until softened and lightly browned.
Add ginger, tomato paste and chopped tomatoes; cook 10–12 minutes until the tomatoes collapse and oil begins to show around the edges.
Add chile, beans and bean liquid. Simmer 15–20 minutes.
Checkpoint: sauce should cling to beans and look glossy, not watery.
Taste for salt and chile, then keep warm.
Slice ripe plantains and fry in shallow neutral oil until caramelized brown on both sides.
Serve red red with fried plantain and remaining fresh onion if desired.
sources: Ghana Tourism Authority — Ghanaian food culture
Fringe Table — Maghreb & West Africa guide

name: Haitian Legim
imageAlt: Illustrative eggplant and cabbage, central vegetables in Haitian legim
imageCredit: Illustrative vegetable image via Wikimedia Commons; not a verified photo of the finished Haitian dish.
summary: Haitian legim, a thick vegetable stew of eggplant, cabbage, chayote and greens seasoned with epis and often enriched with beef.
lead: Vegetables are cooked until soft enough to mash together into the dense, savory texture that makes Haitian legim distinct from a loose soup.
about: Legim is a Haitian vegetable stew whose identity comes from cooking several vegetables until tender and partially mashing them into a thick, unified mixture. Eggplant, cabbage, chayote and leafy greens are common, while beef, crab or other proteins may be included. Epis supplies the aromatic foundation.
story: Legim reflects the vegetable-rich side of Haitian home cooking and is commonly served with rice or rice and beans. Household versions change with season, region and available produce, so the exact vegetable list is flexible while the mashed, concentrated texture remains important.
caveat: This version uses beef and a common vegetable combination, but Haitian families vary both protein and produce. The texture matters more than an immutable ingredient list.
prepNotes: They need to soften fully without vanishing before you can control the final texture.
Legim should be thick and rustic, not completely smooth.
ingredients: 1 tsp salt, plus more to taste
steps: Marinate beef with half the epis, lime juice and salt for at least 30 minutes.
Brown beef in oil, add tomato paste and remaining epis, then add water or stock and simmer 45 minutes.
Add eggplant, cabbage, chayote and carrots; cover and simmer 30–40 minutes until extremely tender.
Add greens for the final 5 minutes.
Remove beef pieces temporarily and mash vegetables with a potato masher.
Checkpoint: the stew should be thick enough to mound on a spoon while still showing vegetable texture.
Return beef, simmer 10 minutes and adjust salt before serving with rice.

name: Uzbek Lagman
imageAlt: Central Asian lagman noodles with meat and vegetables
imageCredit: Image via Wikimedia Commons; see linked file page for creator and license.
summary: Uzbek lagman: chewy noodles topped with a savory lamb-and-vegetable sauce scented with cumin and chile.
lead: Long noodles meet a wok-like meat and vegetable sauce in one of Central Asia's great hand-pulled noodle traditions.
about: Lagman is a Central Asian noodle family associated especially with Uyghur and Uzbek cooking. Uzbek versions often pair long chewy noodles with a saucy mixture of lamb or beef, peppers, tomato, radish and aromatics. Home cooks can use purchased fresh wheat noodles while preserving the structure of noodles plus intensely seasoned topping.
story: Lagman reflects centuries of exchange across Central Asia, where wheat-noodle traditions moved alongside trade and migration. Hand-pulling the noodles is a specialized craft; this version focuses on the sauce and uses sturdy fresh noodles so the dish remains practical without pretending packaged noodles are identical to a skilled lagman pull.
caveat: Uyghur and Uzbek lagman traditions overlap but are not interchangeable. This page uses an Uzbek-style meat-and-vegetable topping and a home shortcut for noodles.
prepNotes: Soft pasta disappears under the sauce.
Lagman should keep distinct pieces rather than become stew mush.
Browning first creates depth before liquid is added.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb lamb or beef, cut small
steps: Brown meat in hot oil in batches until deeply colored.
Add onion, cumin and garlic; cook until fragrant.
Add peppers, radish or carrot and tomatoes; cook 5 minutes.
Add stock and chile, then simmer 30–40 minutes until meat is tender.
Checkpoint: vegetables should remain distinct and the sauce should be loose enough to coat noodles generously.
Boil noodles until chewy-tender, drain and divide among bowls.
Spoon meat, vegetables and broth over noodles and finish with cilantro.
shop: fresh hand pulled style wheat noodles
sources: Fringe Table — Caucasus, Central & West Asia guide

name: Tibetan Shapale
imageCredit: Image via Wikimedia Commons; see linked file page for creator and license.
summary: Tibetan shapale: pan-fried rounds of dough filled with juicy seasoned beef or yak-style filling, crisp outside and tender within.
lead: A juicy meat filling is sealed inside sturdy wheat dough and shallow-fried until the seams blister and the crust turns deeply golden.
about: Shapale, also written sha phaley, is a Tibetan filled bread or pastry commonly made with seasoned meat enclosed in wheat dough and fried. The filling is intentionally juicy, while the dough must be sturdy enough to contain that moisture without becoming thick and bready.
story: Tibetan diaspora restaurants and community cookbooks preserve shapale as both everyday comfort food and a popular restaurant dish. Shapes and fillings vary, and yak meat may be used where available; beef is the practical substitute used here.
caveat: This home version uses beef and shallow frying. Regional and household methods vary in filling, shape and frying depth.
prepNotes: Soft dough is harder to seal around a juicy filling.
Cold filling is easier to portion and reduces leaking.
Pinch or crimp the entire edge before frying.
steps: Mix flour, salt and enough water to make a firm smooth dough; rest 30 minutes.
Combine beef, onion, scallion, ginger, garlic, soy sauce and pepper; chill 20 minutes.
Divide dough into 12 pieces and roll each into a 5-inch round.
Place filling on one half, fold over and crimp tightly.
Checkpoint: no filling or juice should touch the sealing edge.
Shallow-fry over medium heat 4–5 minutes per side until deep golden.
Check one pastry: filling should reach 160°F and dough should be cooked through without raw bands.
sources: Tibetan Nuns Project — Tibetan food and community recipes
Fringe Table — Himalayas & South Asia guide

name: Vietnamese Bánh Xèo
imageAlt: Vietnamese bánh xèo savory rice crepe
imageCredit: Image via Wikimedia Commons; see linked file page for creator and license.
summary: Vietnamese bánh xèo: crisp turmeric rice crepes folded around pork, shrimp and bean sprouts and eaten with herbs and nước chấm.
lead: A thin rice batter hits a hot pan with a loud sizzle—the sound behind the name—and crisps around a fresh, savory filling.
about: Bánh xèo are Vietnamese savory rice crepes colored with turmeric and commonly filled with pork, shrimp and bean sprouts. They are eaten wrapped in lettuce and herbs with dipping sauce. The batter should spread very thinly so the crepe becomes lacy and crisp rather than pancake-soft.
story: Regional bánh xèo differ substantially in size, coconut milk and fillings. Southern versions are often larger and may include coconut milk, while central versions can be smaller and crisper. This version follows a southern-leaning home method while keeping the regional variation explicit.
caveat: Vietnamese bánh xèo are regionally diverse. This is a southern-style home adaptation, not a universal national formula.
prepNotes: Thirty minutes helps rice flour hydrate.
The characteristic crispness begins with immediate sizzling.
Too much filling steams the crepe instead of crisping it.
steps: Whisk rice flour, cornstarch, turmeric, salt, coconut milk and water until smooth; rest 30 minutes and stir in scallions.
Sear pork and shrimp in a hot nonstick skillet until nearly cooked; remove.
Add a teaspoon oil and pour a thin layer of batter, immediately swirling to the edges.
Add a small amount of pork, shrimp and sprouts to one half; cover 1 minute.
Uncover and cook until edges pull away and the underside is crisp and golden.
Checkpoint: the crepe should crackle at the rim and fold without turning gummy.
Fold, slide onto a plate and serve immediately with lettuce, herbs and nước chấm.
sources: Serious Eats — bánh xèo technique and context
